TMS Relay Setting: How the Time Multiplier Changes Trip Time

TMS relay setting is the time multiplier setting of an IDMT relay. It multiplies the base time from the curve equation, so it moves the whole curve up or down in time without changing its shape. Typical numerical relays allow TMS from about 0.05 to 1.0 in small steps.

For the standard inverse curve at PSM 10, the base time is 0.14 ÷ (10^0.02 − 1) = 2.97 s. The trip time is simply TMS × 2.97 s.

Choosing TMS for an upstream relay

  1. Find the trip time of the downstream relay at the maximum fault level it sees. Here it is 0.30 s at TMS 0.1.
  2. Add the grading margin, about 0.3 to 0.4 s with numerical relays. Using 0.35 s gives a target of 0.65 s.
  3. Calculate the PSM of the upstream relay for the same fault from its own CT ratio and plug setting.
  4. Find the base time from the curve equation at that PSM. If it is also 2.97 s, TMS = 0.65 ÷ 2.97 = 0.22.
  5. Round to the nearest available setting and check the margin again at minimum fault current.

A larger TMS gives more selectivity but slower clearing, so the smallest TMS that keeps the margin is the best choice.
